name: Love and Strife as cosmic forces
plain_explanation: Empedocles held that the four elements are combined by a force called Love and separated by an opposed force called Strife, and that the history of the universe is a repeating cycle in which first Love, then Strife, gains the upper hand.
precise_definition: Two primitive, elemental forces, ranked by Empedocles alongside earth, air, fire, and water themselves, that respectively unite and separate the elements; their alternating dominance produces a cosmic cycle including a 'Golden Age' when Love was completely victorious and an opposite extreme when Strife is wholly dominant.
why_it_mattered: Provides a 'softened' alternative to Heraclitus's doctrine that strife alone produces change: for Empedocles it is the interplay of two opposed principles, not strife by itself, that generates the world's changes, addressing Parmenides' objections to change while still accounting for motion.
examples: The Golden Age, when Love was completely victorious and men worshipped only the Cyprian Aphrodite
Plato's summary in the Sophist, contrasting the 'severer' Ionian/Heraclitean view of perpetual strife with the 'gentler' Sicilian view (Empedocles) of alternating Love and Strife
competing_positions: Heraclitus's view that strife alone, without a counterbalancing unifying force, produces the world's harmony
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly modeled on, and named after, the goddess of Love (Aphrodite) and a personified Strife; described within a cyclical mythic framework including a Golden Age.
